newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police attack protesters, scores wounded.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police attack protesters, scores wounded.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's security police attacked thousands of peaceful demonstrators overnight, injuring more than 100 in the bloodiest political violence seen for years in Belgrade.

Vuk Draskovic, co-leader of the opposition coalition, urged followers to arm themselves in "self-defence" for another demonstration on Monday, a call that could signal an ominous turn to almost three months of peaceful pro-democracy rallies.

But Zoran Djindjic, another opposition leader, cautioned demonstrators who have been protesting for three months against alleged election fraud not to resort to violence and give Milosevic a pretext for declaring emergency rule.

Demonstrations resumed on Monday afternoon with 25,000 students massing before the separate opposition bloc rally was to begin. The students demanded a meeting with the public prosecutor, which was refused. Riot police were not in sight.
Vesna Pesic, third member of the opposition's leadership troika, said she feared the sudden police crackdown might mean a state of emergency was just around the corner.

Pesic, a veteran human rights campaigner in her 50s who was clubbed in the back and thigh by police, said the governing Socialists needed a legal tool to pre-empt a pending court ruling that might confirm opposition wins in local elections.
Emergency rule would also override the expiry on Tuesday of the current Socialist-led city council's mandate, she said.
State television (RTS) said police struck on Sunday night only to clear crowds who for three hours had blocked the Brankov Bridge, one of Belgrade's major traffic arteries.

Protesters of the Zajedno (Together) coalition had been trying to file across the bridge to a central square for their usual evening rally, a fact not mentioned by RTS. Traffic would have been jammed for 30 minutes at most if they had been allowed to proceed, as they had on several previous nights.
Six weeks ago the Interior Ministry banned marches that block traffic but has only sporadically enforced the measure.

Police in helmets and body armour turned central Belgrade into a battleground, repeatedly charging marchers demanding the restoration of opposition victories in elections in 14 large Serbian municipalities, including the capital.

Most of the 20,000 marchers gathering for the 77th day of protests quickly dispersed in the face of truncheon charges backed up by water cannon, some of whose salvos were apparently laced with a tear-gas chemical.
But some stood their ground in subzero temperatures, retaliating by hurling stones, bricks and bottles.

Local journalists said such aggressive forays by security forces had not been seen in Belgrade since 1991 when Milosevic called in tanks to quell protests against autocratic leftist rule dating back to World War Two.

Doctors at two Belgrade emergency clinics said almost 100 people were admitted for treatment of injuries ranging from limb fractures to broken teeth. Ambulances also tended to countless minor casualties in the streets.

Opposition activists vowed they would not be intimidated by the police assault and summoned supporters to another rally at 3 p.m. (1400 gmt). "All of Belgrade must go into the streets. Our protest will be peaceful but all participants must take with them something to defend themselves," said Draskovic.
"There can be no more Gandhi-style resistance to this madness," Draskovic told independent student Radio Index.
But he is known to make inflammatory statements and his stress on "self-defence" was likely to be taken seriously only by militants in his Serbian Renewal Movement.

France, Germany and Britain condemned the police action as Western support for democracy campaigners in Serbia grew. The French government, in a significant policy switch, invited the three Zajedno leaders to visit Paris as soon as possible.
"(France) solemnly warns the Serbian authorities against a slide into violence which can only lead to a disastrous outcome," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said.
He demanded that Milosevic abide by the conclusions of an OSCE mission that investigated the elections in Serbia and verified that the opposition had won them legitimately.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Milosevic's authoritarianism was jeopardising any chance for federal Yugoslavia, which groups Serbia and tiny Montenegro, to gain economically vital links to the European Union.
Djindjic said the "irrational" police rampage showed Milosevic had lost his nerve. "It is proof that our rallies have been successful in driving him up against a wall.

"We shall continue with our peaceful protests because justice and truth is on our side," he told Reuters. "We have no reason to resort to force, but the street is the only way left for us to express our (will)."
Until now, Socialist authorities had seemed indecisive in the face of unrelenting protests, hesitating to use violence that might provoke renewed international isolation of Serbia.
Senior churchmen and soldiers have joined the opposition in demanding recognition of the November 17 election results.
